title: Compatible intersections of small enriched cellular slices
statement:
Fix a universe $\mathcal U$; smallness is relative to it and all Hom sets are small. Colimits mean [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. An infinite cardinal $\kappa$ is regular if unions of fewer than $\kappa$ sets of size less than $\kappa$ have size less than $\kappa$. A category is $\kappa$-filtered if every diagram with fewer than $\kappa$ morphisms has a cocone. An object is $\kappa$-presentable if its ordinary Hom functor preserves small $\kappa$-filtered colimits. Locally $\kappa$-presentable means cocomplete and generated under these colimits by a small family of $\kappa$-presentable objects. Let $\kappa$ be uncountable regular and $\mathcal A$ an ordinary locally $\kappa$-presentable category enriched, tensored and cotensored over small simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set, def-coef-simplicial-tensor-cotensor]. Let $I$ be a small simplicial category with fewer than $\kappa$ objects: its simplicial Hom objects have associative composition and identity vertices. Enriched functors $F:I\to\mathcal A$ have actions $I(i,j)\otimes F_i\to F_j$ satisfying unit and composition laws; enriched transformations commute with these actions as simplicial maps. Assume that each functor $I(i,j)\otimes-:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$ takes $\kappa$-presentable objects to $\kappa$-presentable objects.

Let $L$ be any arrow class with $\kappa$-presentable endpoints, and let $f:F\to G$ be an enriched transformation. For each $i$, fix a $\kappa$-good $L$-cellular tree with root $F_i$, small well-founded indexing poset $T_i$, and colimit $G_i$ realizing $f_i$, as in [def-coef-good-cellular-tree]. For downward-closed $B\subseteq T_i$ write $Y_i(B)$ for its colimit in $F_i/\mathcal A$. A slice consists of downward-closed subsets $B_i\subseteq T_i$ and enriched diagram actions on the objects $Y_i(B_i)$ making $F\to Y(B)\to G$ enriched transformations with composite $f$. A slice extends another if its subsets contain the other's and the canonical tree-colimit maps form an enriched transformation. Given a slice $M$ with subsets $A_i$ and subsets $E_i\subseteq T_i$ with $|E_i|<\kappa$, there exist slices $N,N'$ with subsets $B_i$ and $B_i\cap A_i$, respectively, such that $E_i\subseteq B_i$, $|B_i|<\kappa$, and $N'$ extends to both $N$ and $M$. Thus the intersection maps commute with every simplicial action. The roots $F_i$ and the objects $G_i,Y_i(A_i)$ need not be presentable.

source.place: HTT Lemmas A.3.3.15-A.3.3.16, printed pp.879-882, specialized to simplicial enrichment; tensor presentability is the consequence of condition (iii) used by the proof. Read online 2026-10-17; archival HTT WANTED. No Stacks tag states this enriched categorical lemma.

proof.text: Write compositions right to left. Put $K_{ij}=I(i,j)$, with unit $e_i:\Delta^0\to K_{ii}$ and composition $c_{ijk}:K_{jk}\times K_{ij}\to K_{ik}$. Denote the given actions by $a^F_{ij},a^G_{ij},a^M_{ij}$. We use the canonical identifications $\Delta^0\otimes Z=Z$ and $(K\times H)\otimes Z=K\otimes(H\otimes Z)$: their maps into any $W$ are the same maps into $\underline{\operatorname{Map}}(Z,W)$ by the representing isomorphisms and simplicial currying. Uniqueness of representing objects supplies these identifications and their coherent unit and associativity maps. For fixed $K$, $K\otimes-$ preserves ordinary colimits: maps $K\otimes\operatorname{colim}Z_d\to W$ correspond successively to maps $\operatorname{colim}Z_d\to W^K$, compatible maps $Z_d\to W^K$, and compatible maps $K\otimes Z_d\to W$. Thus it preserves the tree pushouts and the chain colimits used below.

source.place: A.3.3.15, pp.879-881: tensor and colimit universal properties expanded.

proof.text: For any object $R$, the category $R/\mathcal A$ has small Hom sets and all small colimits. To compute a colimit, adjoin to its underlying diagram an initial indexing vertex with value $R$ and all structural arrows; cocones on this augmented diagram are exactly cocones under $R$. For a nonempty filtered diagram, its underlying colimit already carries the root map: the maps out of $R$ agree at a common successor. Hence forgetting the root creates filtered colimits. For a $\kappa$-presentable $P$, the free object $\Phi_R(P)=(R\to R\amalg P)$ is presentable under $R$, because $\operatorname{Hom}_{R/\mathcal A}(\Phi_R(P),Z)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(P,UZ)$. The initial object $1_R$ is presentable as well: its Hom functor is singleton, and a nonempty filtered colimit of singleton sets is singleton by the elementwise criterion.

source.place: A.3.3.15, p.879: relative compactness under an arbitrary root.

proof.text: Fix a downward-closed $D\subseteq T_i$ of size less than $\kappa$. For $W$ equal to the identity functor, $K_{ij}\otimes-$, or $K_{jk}\otimes(K_{ij}\otimes-)$, apply $W$ to the restricted cellular tree. Its root is $R=WF_i$, its cell endpoints are $WP_t,WQ_t$, and its restricted colimit is $WY_i(D)$, by Step 1. These endpoints are presentable: this is the original endpoint hypothesis for $W=1$, the tensor hypothesis for a single tensor, and its iteration for a double tensor. Regard this tree in $R/\mathcal A$ with root $1_R$ and endpoints $\Phi_R(WP_t),\Phi_R(WQ_t)$. Its pushout squares are the required squares under $R$: a map out is a map out of the predecessor object and a map from $WQ_t$ agreeing on $WP_t$. Step 2 makes its root and endpoints presentable. Apply [lem-coef-small-tree-presentable-vertices] in this cocomplete category on the inherited small well-founded poset $D$. It follows that $WY_i(D)$ is presentable under $WF_i$. This applies also to $D\cap A_i$ and to the empty set. It asserts no ordinary presentability of $F_i$ or $Y_i(D)$.

source.place: A.3.3.15, p.879: the compactness assertion after tensoring, reduced to the small-tree theorem.

proof.text: Let $\mathscr P$ be the small poset of families $D=(D_i)$ of downward-closed subsets of $T_i$ of size less than $\kappa$. It is small because all $T_i$ and the object set of $I$ are small. The downward closure of $E_i$ is $\bigcup_{t\in E_i}(\{t\}\cup(T_i)_{<t})$, of size less than $\kappa$ by goodness and regularity; choose it as $B_{0,i}$. Unions of fewer than $\kappa$ families give upper bounds in $\mathscr P$, so this poset and every tail above a family are $\kappa$-filtered. On any such tail, $D\mapsto Y_j(D_j)$ has colimit $G_j$, and $D\mapsto Y_j(D_j\cap A_j)$ has colimit $M_j$. Indeed any vertex of $T_j$, or of $A_j$, lies in a small downward closure; union with the tail's lower bound provides an index there. A cocone on these pieces therefore gives a leg at every vertex, independent of choices by taking unions. Every order arrow is in a single piece, so these legs are a cocone on the entire restricted tree. Restriction gives the inverse correspondence. Step 2 gives the same presentations under any root $R\to F_j$.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16, pp.879-882: the small-piece filtered presentations and tails.

proof.text: For any of the relatively presentable sources $Z=WY_i(D_i)$ of Step 3, a map under $R=WF_i$ to $G_j$, or to $M_j$, factors through a member of the appropriate presentation in Step 4. Apply the presentability of $Z$ and clause (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-filtered-colimit-sets-elementwise]. Two such maps to stages agreeing in the total object become equal at a larger stage by clauses (2)-(3). Every application below uses the same specified map from $R$ to the target root $F_j$. Fewer than $\kappa$ factorizations and equality witnesses can be imposed together by taking a common upper bound in $\mathscr P$. Only pairs and triples of objects index the requirements, so there are fewer than $\kappa$ of them: for an infinite object cardinal $\theta<\kappa$, $\theta^2=\theta$ and then $\theta^3=\theta$ by [lem-coef-infinite-cardinal-square-power]; finite object sets are immediate. We factor whole action maps with sources $K_{ij}\otimes Z$, not one map for each simplex, so no bound on the number of simplices of $K_{ij}$ is needed.

source.place: A.3.3.15 compactness argument, pp.879-881; A.3.3.16, p.882: simultaneous witnesses.

proof.text:
We construct increasing families $B_n\in\mathscr P$. Put $X_n^i=Y_i(B_{n,i})$, $H_n^i=Y_i(B_{n,i}\cap A_i)$, with canonical maps $x_n^i:X_n^i\to X_{n+1}^i$, $h_n^i:H_n^i\to H_{n+1}^i$, $k_n^i:H_n^i\to X_n^i$. Write $g_n^i:X_n^i\to G_i$, $m_n^i:H_n^i\to M_i$, $q_i:M_i\to G_i$, and root maps $r_n^i:F_i\to X_n^i$, $s_n^i:F_i\to H_n^i$. At stage $n$ choose partial action maps $u_n^{ij}:K_{ij}\otimes X_n^i\to X_{n+1}^j$ and $v_n^{ij}:K_{ij}\otimes H_n^i\to H_{n+1}^j$ satisfying
$$g_{n+1}^ju_n^{ij}=a^G_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes g_n^i),\quad m_{n+1}^jv_n^{ij}=a^M_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes m_n^i),$$
$$u_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes r_n^i)=r_{n+1}^ja^F_{ij},\quad v_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes s_n^i)=s_{n+1}^ja^F_{ij}.$$
These are partial actions; the stages are not asserted to be enriched diagrams. Step 5 factors the two global action maps for every pair $(i,j)$ under $K_{ij}\otimes F_i$, where the target root is specified by $a^F_{ij}$. A common upper family gives preliminary maps $\widetilde u^{ij},\widetilde v^{ij}$ into $Y_j(C_j),Y_j(C_j\cap A_j)$ with $C\supseteq B_n$.

Enlarge $C$ so that the intersection and unit equations hold:
$$k_{n+1}^jv_n^{ij}=u_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes k_n^i),\qquad u_n^{ii}(e_i\otimes X_n^i)=x_n^i,\qquad v_n^{ii}(e_i\otimes H_n^i)=h_n^i.$$
Here $x_n,h_n,k_{n+1}$ denote the canonical maps into the final enlarged family. For the first equation the preliminary two maps out of $K_{ij}\otimes H_n^i$ agree in $G_j$: the $M$ route becomes $q_ja^M_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes m_n^i)=a^G_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes q_im_n^i)$ by enriched naturality of $q$, and $q_im_n^i=g_n^ik_n^i$. They agree on the root by the root equations. The two unit comparisons agree in $G_i$ and $M_i$ by the unit laws for those actions, and agree under $F_i$ by the unit law for $F$. Step 5 equalizes these pairs with respectively the single-tensor and identity sources of Step 3. Enlargements only postcompose the preliminary maps, so the root and global equations remain true.

source.place: A.3.3.15 unit laws and A.3.3.16(f), pp.879-882: equality witnesses for units and intersection.

proof.text:
For $n\geq1$, additionally require the transition equations
$$u_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes x_{n-1}^i)=x_n^ju_{n-1}^{ij},\qquad v_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes h_{n-1}^i)=h_n^jv_{n-1}^{ij}.$$
Before enlargement, the first pair of maps into $Y_j(C_j)$ has common source $K_{ij}\otimes X_{n-1}^i$. Their images in $G_j$ are both $a^G_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes g_{n-1}^i)$ by the previously imposed global equation and $g_n^ix_{n-1}^i=g_{n-1}^i$. Their restrictions to $K_{ij}\otimes F_i$ agree by the root equation. The second pair likewise agrees in $M_j$ with common source $K_{ij}\otimes H_{n-1}^i$ and the same root. Step 5 makes all these equations literal after enlargement.

source.place: A.3.3.15 second compatibility diagram, p.881; A.3.3.16(d)-(e), pp.881-882.

proof.text:
For every triple $(i,j,l)$ and $n\geq1$, impose
$$u_n^{jl}(K_{jl}\otimes u_{n-1}^{ij})=u_n^{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes x_{n-1}^i),$$
$$v_n^{jl}(K_{jl}\otimes v_{n-1}^{ij})=v_n^{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes h_{n-1}^i).$$
The first equation has source $K_{jl}\otimes K_{ij}\otimes X_{n-1}^i$ and target $X_{n+1}^l$, using the product-tensor identification of Step 1. For preliminary maps into $Y_l(C_l)$ its two sides have images in $G_l$ respectively
$$a^G_{jl}(K_{jl}\otimes a^G_{ij})(K_{jl}\otimes K_{ij}\otimes g_{n-1}^i),\qquad a^G_{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes g_{n-1}^i).$$
These agree by the composition law of $G$. Their root restrictions agree by that of $F$. Replacing $X,u,g,G$ by $H,v,m,M$ proves equality in $M_l$ for the second pair with the same root restriction. The double-tensor sources are presentable under $K_{jl}\otimes K_{ij}\otimes F_i$ by Step 3. Therefore Step 5 supplies equality witnesses. No equation is obtained by canceling a map to $G_l$ or $M_l$.

source.place: A.3.3.15 first compatibility diagram, pp.880-881; A.3.3.16(d)-(e), p.882: composition equations.

proof.text: Take a common upper member for the preliminary family $C$ and all witnesses in Steps 7-9; denote it $B_{n+1}$. Postcompose the preliminary maps to this family and call them $u_n,v_n$. The number of witnesses is less than $\kappa$ by Step 5, so $B_{n+1}\in\mathscr P$. Each imposed equation survives this enlargement: both sides postcompose by the same canonical target map, and the maps $u_{n-1},v_{n-1}$ in Steps 8-9 stay fixed. The intersection squares of canonical tree maps commute by colimit uniqueness. At $n=0$ impose only Steps 6-7; there are no negative-stage maps. This starts the recursion at the prescribed downward closures $B_0$ and completes its induction over all natural numbers.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16, pp.880-882: completing each recursive stage without monomorphisms.

proof.text:
Put $B_i=\bigcup_{n<\omega}B_{n,i}$ and $C_i=B_i\cap A_i=\bigcup_{n<\omega}(B_{n,i}\cap A_i)$. They are downward-closed, $E_i\subseteq B_i$, and $|B_i|<\kappa$ since $\kappa$ is uncountable regular. Put $X^i=Y_i(B_i)$ and $H^i=Y_i(C_i)$. They are colimits of the chains $X_n^i,H_n^i$, with legs $\xi_n^i,\eta_n^i$: each vertex and order arrow in either union occurs at a finite stage, so the cocone argument of Step 4 applies. Tensoring with $K_{ij}$ preserves these chain colimits by Step 1. Thus the transition equations of Step 8 define maps
$$U^{ij}:K_{ij}\otimes X^i\to X^j,\qquad V^{ij}:K_{ij}\otimes H^i\to H^j$$
uniquely by $U^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes\xi_n^i)=\xi_{n+1}^ju_n^{ij}$ and $V^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes\eta_n^i)=\eta_{n+1}^jv_n^{ij}$.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16 conclusion, pp.881-882: countable unions and amalgamation.

proof.text:
The unit equations of Step 7 give $U^{ii}(e_i\otimes X^i)\xi_n^i=\xi_{n+1}^ix_n^i=\xi_n^i$, proving the unit law by colimit uniqueness. On the leg $K_{jl}\otimes K_{ij}\otimes\xi_n^i$, the composite $U^{jl}(K_{jl}\otimes U^{ij})$ becomes
$$\xi_{n+2}^lu_{n+1}^{jl}(K_{jl}\otimes u_n^{ij})=\xi_{n+2}^lu_{n+1}^{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes x_n^i)=\xi_{n+1}^lu_n^{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes X_n^i).$$
This is the restriction of $U^{il}(c_{ijl}\otimes X^i)$. Double tensoring preserves the chain colimit by Step 1, so these restrictions prove the composition law. Substitution of $H,V,v,h,\eta$ for $X,U,u,x,\xi$ proves both laws for $V$. Consequently these maps define enriched functors on $X$ and $H$, with all simplicial degrees controlled by tensor maps rather than vertexwise equations.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16 conclusion, pp.881-882: enriched unit and composition laws on colimit legs.

proof.text:
Let $r_i:F_i\to X^i$, $s_i:F_i\to H^i$, $g_i:X^i\to G_i$, $m_i:H^i\to M_i$ be the canonical maps. The root equations of Step 6 give $U^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes r_i)=r_ja^F_{ij}$ and $V^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes s_i)=s_ja^F_{ij}$, by expressing $r_i,s_i$ at any stage. For example, on $K_{ij}\otimes\xi_n^i$ the global equation gives
$$g_jU^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes\xi_n^i)=g_{n+1}^ju_n^{ij}=a^G_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes g_n^i).$$
The colimit property proves $g_jU^{ij}=a^G_{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes g_i)$; replacing $g,G,U,\xi,u$ by $m,M,V,\eta,v$ proves the equation for $m$. Hence $F\to X\to G$ and $F\to H\to M\to G$ are enriched factorizations of $f$; their composites are $f$ on the root by the tree's structural maps. Thus $N=(B,U)$ and $N'=(C,V)$ are slices, and the canonical map $N'\to M$ is enriched.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16 conclusion, pp.881-882: the enriched maps under F and over G.

proof.text:
Let $k_i:H^i\to X^i$ be the canonical map from the intersection colimit, so $k_i\eta_n^i=\xi_n^ik_n^i$. The intersection equation of Step 7 yields
$$U^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes k_i)(K_{ij}\otimes\eta_n^i)=\xi_{n+1}^ju_n^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes k_n^i)=\xi_{n+1}^jk_{n+1}^jv_n^{ij}=k_jV^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes\eta_n^i).$$
Tensor preservation and colimit uniqueness imply $U^{ij}(K_{ij}\otimes k_i)=k_jV^{ij}$. Thus $N'\to N$ is enriched, as is $N'\to M$ from Step 13. The underlying subsets are exactly $C_i=B_i\cap A_i$, so both maps are the canonical extension maps required. Their two composites to $G$ agree on every tree leg. Empty trees and empty intersections give the root object, so the same root equations apply; with no objects in $I$ the families and actions are empty and the conclusion is vacuous.

source.place: A.3.3.16 conclusion, p.882: both canonical intersection maps respect every simplicial action.
